USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the 90-day G20 window open and negotiate through the March 1 deadline without new tariff hikes, rollbacks, or a purchases-only settlement. Insist that any deal include enforceable structural commitments on IP, forced tech transfer, non-tariff barriers, and cyber theft, with verification—treat Chinese purchase pledges as a down payment, not the deal. Keep the scheduled List 3 hike to 25% as unused leverage; do not trade the Huawei/Meng criminal process for tariff relief.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is a mild US opportunity, not a crisis. Washington already has 25% tariffs on ~$50B and 10% on ~$200B of Chinese goods, and the Jan 1, 2019 List 3 hike to 25% was suspended only for the 90-day talks (timeline 2018-09-24, 2018-12-01). China is under more immediate pressure: official 2018 GDP slowed to 6.6% (28-year low), Q4 to 6.4%, December exports/imports contracted, and Guangdong factories were cutting hours ahead of Lunar New Year. That is leverage. US costs are real but not systemic: China’s 25% soybean tariff cut Jan–Oct 2018 US soy exports to China ~63%, Mississippi stockpiles built up, and Midwest ag-loan stress rose; UMCSENT fell to 91.2 in January and the 10-year yield dropped to 2.70% after the December risk-off (VIX peaked at 36.07 on 2018-12-24). Those hits argue against further escalation during talks, not for conceding. High-level talks on 2019-01-30 still show purchase commitments advancing while enforcement and structural IP/tech-transfer issues remain unresolved—the same pattern as the May 19, 2018 truce that collapsed ten days later when the US refused a purchases-only pause. Commerce Secretary Ross said the sides were still “miles away” on structural reform and penalties. DOJ’s Jan 28 Huawei/Meng indictments and extradition request (White House: “totally separate”) raise the political temperature and China has already detained two Canadians, so mixing criminal process into the tariff bargain would both weaken US legal posture and invite hostage dynamics. Second-order: hiking List 3 now would likely trigger matching Chinese retaliation and blow up the only live channel; a May-style purchase deal would leave the Section 301 findings unaddressed and invite another collapse. Negotiate, hold the existing tariff stock, and make enforcement the test of any text.
key_factors: 90-day G20 truce still open; List 3 remains at 10% with unused 25% hike as leverage
China 2018 growth at 28-year low and December trade contraction increase Beijing's incentive to deal
US farm-belt retaliation (soy exports -63%, stockpiles, rising ag-loan stress) is the main domestic cost
Talks advancing on purchases but not on structural IP/tech-transfer or enforcement—same failure mode as May 2018
Huawei/Meng DOJ case is a parallel legal track that should not be bargained for tariff relief

sources_cited.excerpt: G20 Buenos Aires dinner: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window. Planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended (tariffs remain at 10%). Same day: Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou.
Lighthizer and Mnuchin in Beijing for high-level talks. Purchase commitments discussed; enforcement and structural IP/tech-transfer issues unresolved.
US and China release joint statement after talks: China agrees to significantly increase purchases of US goods and services. Mnuchin says trade war is on hold.
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
List 3 takes effect at 10%. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
US DOJ unseals fraud and sanctions-related charges against Huawei and Meng; US formally requests Meng's extradition from Canada.
University of Michigan consumer sentiment fell to 91.2 in January 2019 from 100.1 in September 2018.
10-year Treasury yield 2.70% on 2019-01-30, down from a November peak near 3.24%.
VIX closed 17.66 on 2019-01-30 after spiking to 36.07 on 2018-12-24.
US goods imports from China fell to $41.3B in January 2019 from $49.9B in September, a 17% decline over the window.
China's 2018 GDP growth slowed to 6.6%, the lowest in 28 years; Q4 growth 6.4%. December exports and imports unexpectedly shrank.
Wilbur Ross: we're miles away from a resolution; issues are not just soy/LNG purchases but structural reforms and enforcement mechanisms/penalties.
January 7–9 Beijing talks: more progress on China's purchase pledge than on structural changes; USTR stressed verification and enforcement.
US soybean exports to China Jan–Oct 2018 were 63% lower than the same period in 2017 after China's 25% retaliatory tariff.
White House: Huawei charges are a totally separate process from trade negotiations; China had already detained Canadians after Meng's arrest.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Stay at the table through the remainder of the 90-day window and keep high-level talks with Lighthizer/Mnuchin open. Signal willingness to specify large, verifiable purchases of U.S. agriculture, energy, and manufactures to shrink the bilateral imbalance, but do not lock in those purchases—or any structural rewrite of industrial policy—until Washington puts a matching tariff freeze or rollback on the table. Do not add new tariff or hostage-style retaliation during this window; further escalation now would make the March 1 List-3 hike to 25% more likely, not less.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high but not existential. Combined U.S. Section 301 coverage is already ~$250B (Lists 1–2 at 25%, List 3 at 10% since 24 Sep 2018), and the G20 pause only delayed—did not cancel—the scheduled List-3 jump to 25% if there is no agreement by early March. That is a direct hit on the export machine: U.S. customs imports from China fell from $49.9B in Sep 2018 to $41.3B in Jan 2019 (−17%), and contemporaneous reporting shows 2018 GDP at 6.6% (slowest since 1990), Q4 at 6.4%, December exports/imports contracting, and Guangdong factories shutting early as orders dry up. Firm-level targeting has also jumped: ZTE was cut off in Apr 2018, and on 28 Jan 2019 DOJ unsealed fraud/sanctions charges against Huawei and Meng and formally requested extradition—the same week Liu He is in talks—while Beijing already detained Kovrig and Spavor. That maps near the CHN +0.5 anchor (export sectors, Huawei, export-hub unemployment risk), but not +1.0: talks are live, the 10%→25% hike is still suspended, and Beijing has policy space (five RRR cuts, pledged tax/infra support, no hard-landing print). Action should stay near zero rather than escalate because a new Chinese tariff or detention wave would give U.S. hawks a pretext to let the March cliff hit and possibly extend tariffs to the remaining ~$267B; the May 2018 purchase-only “trade war on hold” collapsed within days when the White House proceeded with the $50B action. Mid-January talks already showed the split: purchases are discussable, structural IP/tech-transfer/enforcement is not closed, and Ross publicly said the sides are “miles and miles” apart. Concede_purchases is premature—no matching U.S. offer exists. Full rollback or further retaliation would either surrender leverage or blow up the only pause we have. Negotiate: explore de-escalation, keep purchases as bargaining chips, hold the line on “unacceptable” structural items, and use the remaining weeks to test whether Trump’s deal hunger outweighs Lighthizer’s enforcement demands.
key_factors: ~$250B of Chinese exports already under Section 301; List 3 still scheduled to rise from 10% to 25% if the 90-day window fails around 1 Mar 2019
Huawei/Meng criminal charges and extradition request unsealed 28 Jan 2019, coinciding with high-level talks; prior ZTE denial order and Canadian detentions keep a second, non-tariff front open
Real-economy stress: official 2018 GDP 6.6% (28-year low), Dec trade contraction, IMPCH −17% Sep–Jan, Guangdong export-hub order loss and job-risk reports
Talks are live but asymmetric: China can move on purchases; U.S. still demands structural IP/tech-transfer changes plus verification, and the May 2018 purchase truce collapsed

Escalating now raises the odds of the March tariff cliff and a possible further U.S. list; pre-conceding purchases or industrial-policy rewrite without a U.S. tariff concession repeats a failed 2018 sequence
